title: Whole Numbers to 10 000: Counting, Place Value, Comparing and Ordering
seo_title: Grade 4 Whole Numbers to 10 000 Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Count forwards and backwards in 2s, 3s, 5s, 10s, 25s, 50s, 100s between 0 and at least 10 000; order, compare and represent numbers to at least 4-digit numbers; represent odd and even numbers to at least 1 000; recognise the place value of digits in whole numbers to at least 4-digit numbers.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 4 maths worksheets on whole numbers to 10 000: counting in 25s, 50s and 100s, place value, expanded notation, comparing, ordering and odd and even numbers. 100 questions with memos.
key_sub: Compare from the biggest place first.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A 4-digit number has thousands, hundreds, tens and units. In 4 536 the 4 is worth 4 000.
  • Expanded notation: 4 536 = 4 000 + 500 + 30 + 6.
  • To compare, start with the thousands. If they are the same, compare the hundreds, then the tens, then the units.
  • Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
  • When you count in 25s, 50s or 100s, add the same jump each time.

Examples

Example

7 048

7 thousands, 0 hundreds, 4 tens, 8 units

Answer: 7 000 + 40 + 8

Example

Order 3 905, 3 950, 3 059

thousands: all 3

hundreds: 9, 9, 0

Answer: 3 059, 3 905, 3 950

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting on by 1Add the jump (25, 50, 100) each time.
Value or digit?The digit 5 in 4 536 has a value of 500.
Comparing the units firstStart with the biggest place.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 4 say about whole numbers?
faq.a: Count forwards and backwards in 2s, 3s, 5s, 10s, 25s, 50s and 100s to at least 10 000, order, compare and represent numbers to at least 4-digit numbers, and recognise the place value of digits in whole numbers to at least 4-digit numbers.

faq.q: Why do we write 10 000 with a space?
faq.a: South Africa uses a space, not a comma, between groups of three digits.

items.q: Which number is the greatest?
items.e: All four numbers have the same number of digits. Compare from the left. 6 702 and 6 270 are the closest: they first differ in the hundreds place, 7 > 2. So 6 702 is the greatest.

items.q: Which number is the least?
items.e: All four numbers have the same number of digits. Compare from the left. 8 019 and 8 091 are the closest: they first differ in the tens place, 1 < 9. So 8 019 is the least.

items.q: Which number is greater than 6 380?
items.e: Same thousands. Hundreds: 6 803 has 8 hundreds and 6 380 has 3 hundreds. So 6 803 > 6 380. The others are all less than 6 380.

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: 5 602 and 5 620 have the same thousands and hundreds. Tens: 0 tens < 2 tens, so 5 602 < 5 620. The others are false: 3 070 < 3 700, 9 999 < 10 000 and 8 143 > 8 134.

items.q: Which number is between 6 200 and 6 300?
items.e: A number between 6 200 and 6 300 has 6 thousands and 2 hundreds. 6 248 fits. 6 320 is too big, 6 028 is too small and 2 648 is too small.

items.q: Put 5 620, 5 062 and 5 206 in order from least to greatest.

items.q: Use the digits 6, 0, 3 and 8 once each. What is the greatest number you can make?
items.e: Put the biggest digit in the thousands place, then the next biggest: 8, 6, 3, 0. That is 8 630.

items.q: Which number is less than 8 000?
items.e: 7 999 has only 7 thousands. The others have 8 thousands and more, so they are greater than 8 000.

items.q: Put 8 710, 10 000, 8 170 and 8 701 in order from greatest to least.
items.e: 10 000 has 5 digits, so it is the greatest. 8 170 has the fewest hundreds. 8 710 > 8 701 because 1 ten > 0 tens. Order: 10 000, 8 710, 8 701, 8 170.

items.q: Which number is between 4 900 and 5 000?
items.e: A number between 4 900 and 5 000 has 4 thousands and 9 hundreds. 4 960 fits. 5 960 and 5 004 are more than 5 000, and 4 096 is less than 4 900.

items.q: How many counters are there? Is the number odd or even?
items.e: Make pairs: 6 pairs and 1 counter left over. One left over means odd.

items.q: How many counters are there? Is the number odd or even?
items.e: Make pairs: 8 pairs and none left over. Every counter has a partner, so 16 is even.

items.q: How many counters are there? Is the number odd or even?
items.e: Make pairs: 9 pairs and 1 counter left over. One left over means odd.

items.q: How many counters are there? Is the number odd or even?
items.e: Make pairs: 11 pairs and none left over. Every counter has a partner, so 22 is even.

items.q: Is 4 537 odd or even?
items.e: Only the ones digit matters. 4 537 ends in 7, and 7 is odd, so 4 537 is odd. The first digit, 4, does not tell you.

items.q: Is 3 718 odd or even?
items.e: Only the ones digit matters. 3 718 ends in 8, and 8 is even, so 3 718 is even. The first digit, 3, does not tell you.

items.q: Is 6 290 odd or even?
items.e: Only the ones digit matters. 6 290 ends in 0, and 0 is even, so 6 290 is even. The first digit, 6, does not tell you.

items.q: Is 8 005 odd or even?
items.e: Only the ones digit matters. 8 005 ends in 5, and 5 is odd, so 8 005 is odd. The first digit, 8, does not tell you.

items.q: Is 0 odd or even?
items.e: 0 is even. Counting by 2s starts at 0: 0, 2, 4, 6. With 0 objects nothing is left over, and 10, 20 and 300 are even because they end in 0.

items.q: Which number is even?
items.e: Look at the ones digits only: 6, 7, 1, 3. 3 576 ends in 6, so it is even. The first digit does not matter.

items.q: An odd number + an odd number. The answer is …
items.e: Each odd number has 1 left over. The two left-overs make a new pair, so nothing is left: always even. Example: 3 + 5 = 8.

items.q: An even number + an even number. The answer is …
items.e: Both numbers are all pairs, so the total is all pairs: always even. Example: 4 + 6 = 10.

items.q: An odd number + an even number. The answer is …
items.e: The even number is all pairs. The odd number still has 1 left over, so the total is always odd. Example: 7 + 4 = 11.

items.q: An odd number × an odd number. The answer is …
items.e: 3 × 5 is 3 groups of 5. Two of the groups make 10, which is even. One group of 5 is left, and even + odd = odd. So the answer is always odd: 3 × 5 = 15.

items.q: An even number × an odd number. The answer is …
items.e: An even number of equal groups can be paired group with group, so the answer is always even. Example: 4 × 3 = 12.

items.q: An even number × an even number. The answer is …
items.e: Groups of an even number are all pairs, so the answer is always even. Example: 4 × 6 = 24.

items.q: An odd number − an odd number. The answer is …
items.e: Taking away an odd number takes away the 1 left over too, so only pairs are left: always even. Example: 9 − 3 = 6.

items.q: An even number − an odd number. The answer is …
items.e: Taking an odd number from all pairs breaks one pair and leaves 1 over: always odd. Example: 10 − 3 = 7.

items.q: How many counters altogether? Is the total odd or even?
items.e: Red: 7 is odd. Green: 5 is odd. Odd + odd = even, so 7 + 5 = 12 is even. The two left-over counters make a new pair.

items.q: How many counters altogether? Is the total odd or even?
items.e: Red: 6 is even. Green: 9 is odd. Even + odd = odd, so 6 + 9 = 15 is odd.
